How a night of sleep works

Each sleep cycle moves from light sleep through deep sleep to rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when most dreams occur. In early cycles, deep sleep is long and REM is brief at the very end. Toward morning, deep sleep nearly disappears while REM periods can last half an hour or longer. A cue played during REM may become part of a dream, while a cue during deep sleep in an early cycle is more likely to wake you.
Estimated REM share in each cycle
This is an averaged adult hypnogram, not a measurement of your sleep. Real sleep stages vary from person to person and from night to night.

The first REM period usually begins 70–90 minutes after sleep onset. External cues are most effective during REM, especially in the final two or three hours of sleep when REM windows are longest. WBTB and MILD use the same principle: a gentle cue at the right stage can increase the chance of becoming lucid. Playing cues during deep sleep in the early cycles is usually ineffective and may wake you.
S. LaBerge — MILD and WBTB techniques for lucid dream induction.
T. Stumbrys et al. (2013) — review of external stimulation during REM sleep.
K. Konkoly et al. (2021, Current Biology) — two-way communication with sleepers during REM.
D. Aspy et al. — research on MILD and optimal cue timing.

This model is theoretical: the app does not measure sleep stages and only schedules cues using an averaged pattern. If cues disturb your sleep or cause discomfort, turn them off. Keep the volume very low.
